title: Adding and subtracting decimals
blurb: Add and subtract decimals by hand with the points lined up, empty places filled with zeros, and every borrow done correctly.
question: At the campus store you buy hand sanitizer for $2.79, gloves for $8.45 and tape for $3.60, and pay with $20. How much change should you get?

teach.body: Formally, you can only add or subtract digits that have the same place value: tenths with tenths, hundredths with hundredths. Writing the numbers with their decimal points in one column guarantees that, and annexing zeros (12.5 = 12.50) gives every number the same number of places. In plain English: stack the points, fill the gaps with zeros, then add or subtract exactly as with whole numbers.

head: Place
Value
Digit in 3.462
teach.caption: Zeros after the last digit don't change the value: 0.6 = 0.60 = 0.600. A whole number has its point at the end: 20 = 20.00.

items: 12.5 + 3.75 + 0.6: line up the points and fill with zeros: 12.50 + 3.75 + 0.60.
Hundredths: 0 + 5 + 0 = 5. Tenths: 5 + 7 + 6 = 18, write 8, carry 1. Ones: 2 + 3 + 0 + 1 = 6. Tens: 1.
Answer: 16.85. The point drops straight down from the column above.
Borrow 1 from the ones: 15.000 becomes 14 ones, 9 tenths, 9 hundredths, 10 thousandths.

teach.h: Points lined up vs last digits lined up
teach.caption: Lining up the right-hand ends only works when every number has the same number of decimal places.

head: Slip
Wrong answer
Fix
rows: Borrow when the top digit is smaller
The ones digit drops from 7 to 6

teach.text: Two subtraction slips the HESI A2 builds wrong answers from: taking the smaller digit from the larger in each column instead of borrowing (4 − 1.35 → 3.35; it is 2.65), and borrowing without reducing the digit you borrowed from (5.3 − 4.87 → 0.53 or 1.43; it is 0.43). Always check by adding back.

teach.body: Andre Williams, a nursing student, buys sanitizer for $2.79, gloves for $8.45 and tape for $3.60. Total: 2.79 + 8.45 = 11.24; 11.24 + 3.60 = $14.84. Change from $20: 20.00 − 14.84. Borrow across the zeros: 19 ones, 9 tenths, 10 hundredths, so 10 − 4 = 6, 9 − 8 = 1, 19 − 14 = 5: $5.16. Check: 14.84 + 5.16 = 20.00. ✓

items: Line up the decimal points; the point in the answer drops straight down.
Annex zeros so every number has the same number of decimal places (20 = 20.00).
Borrowing across zeros: each zero you pass becomes 9.
Check a subtraction by adding the answer to the number you took away.

summary: You can now add and subtract decimals by hand with the points lined up and zeros annexed, borrow correctly across zeros, and check every difference by adding back. You also recognize the misaligned and missed-borrow answers the HESI A2 offers.

A.q: A nurse had a 2 L bag of saline. She used 0.65 L, then another 0.4 L. How much saline is left?

whyNot.1: 1.31 subtracts 0.04 instead of 0.4: the 4 was lined up in the hundredths place.
whyNot.2: 1.35 is what is left after the first use only, an intermediate step.
whyNot.3: 1.05 comes from a borrowing slip in 2 − 0.65 (1.45 instead of 1.35), then subtracting 0.4.

A.why: Line up the points and fill with zeros: 8.40 + 0.37 + 12.00 = 20.77.

whyNot.0: 8.89 treats 12 as 0.12; a whole number's point is at its right end.
whyNot.1: 13.21 lines up the last digits, adding 0.84 + 0.37 + 12.

A.q: A patient weighed 182.4 lb at admission and 176.85 lb at discharge. How much weight did the patient lose?
A.why: Write 182.4 as 182.40 and subtract with borrowing: 182.40 − 176.85 = 5.55 lb. Check: 176.85 + 5.55 = 182.40.

whyNot.0: 6.55 forgets to reduce the ones digit after borrowing from it (12 − 6 instead of 11 − 6).
whyNot.1: 5.65 forgets to reduce the tenths digit after borrowing for the hundredths (14 − 8 instead of 13 − 8).
whyNot.3: 5.19 reads 182.4 as 182.04, putting the 4 in the hundredths place.

B.q: Lena buys a notebook for $2.49, pens for $5.75 and a planner for $11.30. She pays with a $20 bill. How much change does she get?

whyNot.0: $1.46 forgets to reduce the ones digit to 9 after borrowing from it.
whyNot.2: $11.56 turns each zero in 20.00 into 10 without reducing it to 9 after lending.
whyNot.3: $19.54 is the total cost, not the change.

B.why: Write 9.85 as 9.850: 12.006 − 9.850. Thousandths 6 − 0 = 6; hundredths borrow: 10 − 5 = 5; tenths 9 − 8 = 1; ones 11 − 9 = 2. Answer 2.156. Check: 9.85 + 2.156 = 12.006.

whyNot.0: 2.256 forgets to reduce the tenths digit (0 becomes 9, not 10) after lending.
whyNot.1: 3.156 forgets to reduce the ones digit after borrowing from it.
whyNot.3: 11.021 lines up the last digits and subtracts 0.985 instead of 9.85.

B.q: A patient's hemoglobin rose from 9.8 g/dL to 11.25 g/dL. By how much did it rise?
B.why: 11.25 − 9.80: hundredths 5 − 0 = 5; tenths borrow: 12 − 8 = 4; ones 10 − 9 = 1. Answer 1.45 g/dL. Check: 9.8 + 1.45 = 11.25.

whyNot.1: 2.45 forgets to reduce the ones after borrowing (11 − 9 instead of 10 − 9).
whyNot.2: 2.65 takes the smaller digit from the larger in the tenths column instead of borrowing.
whyNot.3: 10.27 lines up the last digits and subtracts 0.98 instead of 9.8.

C.q: A student has $85.00 on a campus card. She spends $12.48 and $9.75, then adds $40. What is her balance?

whyNot.0: $22.77 subtracts the $40 added instead of adding it.
whyNot.1: $62.77 leaves out the $40 added to the card.
whyNot.2: $102.87 forgets to reduce the tenths digit after borrowing in 72.52 − 9.75.

whyNot.0: 7.33 forgets to reduce the ones after borrowing for the tenths.
whyNot.2: 7.73 takes the smaller digit from the larger in the tenths column (7 − 0) instead of borrowing.
whyNot.3: 10.56 lines up the last digits and subtracts 0.47 instead of 4.7.

C.q: A vial holds 10 mL. Doses of 2.5 mL, 1.75 mL and 3.125 mL are drawn from it. How much is left?

whyNot.0: 3.735 mL turns each zero in 10.000 into 10 without reducing it to 9 after lending.
whyNot.1: 5.75 mL subtracts only the first two doses.
whyNot.3: 7.375 mL is the total drawn, not the amount left.

reteach.title: Decimals are dollars and cents
reteach.question: You check a receipt every time you shop. How does stacking dollars over dollars and cents over cents explain the decimal rules?

blocks.body: On a receipt, $12.50, $3.75 and $0.60 stack with dollars over dollars and cents over cents. Nobody adds 50 cents to 3 dollars by mistake, because the decimal points line up. That is the whole addition rule. Writing $0.6 as $0.60 is just writing 60 cents in full, which is why annexing zeros never changes a value.

head: Item
Price
blocks.caption: Points stacked in one column; $0.60 is the same as $0.6.

items: A cashier finds $20 − $13.22 by counting up from the price.
Change: $6 + $0.78 = $6.78, the same as 20.00 − 13.22 with borrowing. ✓

blocks.text: $3.20 plus 45 cents is $3.65, not 77 cents. Line up the points, never the last digits.

explain.body: Write each number with its point in one column. A whole number's point is at its right end. Fill empty places with zeros, then add.
Give the whole number a decimal point and enough zeros to match, then subtract with borrowing.

test.q: A 7 mL syringe is filled, and 2.36 mL is injected. How much is left in the syringe?

whyNot.0: 5.36 subtracts only the whole number (7 − 2) and keeps the .36.
whyNot.1: 4.74 forgets to reduce the tenths after borrowing for the hundredths.
whyNot.3: 9.36 adds the amounts instead of subtracting.

explain.body: When you borrow across a run of zeros, every zero you pass becomes 9 and only the last place gets 10. 5.000 becomes 4 ones, 9 tenths, 9 hundredths, 10 thousandths.

test.why: 5.000 − 0.008: borrow so the thousandths become 10 and the tenths and hundredths become 9: 4.992. Check: 4.992 + 0.008 = 5.

whyNot.0: 4.002 reduces the ones but leaves the tenths and hundredths at 0 instead of 9.
whyNot.1: 4.92 subtracts 0.08, putting the 8 in the hundredths place.
whyNot.2: 5.008 takes 0 − 8 as 8 instead of borrowing, which adds instead of subtracting.

explain.body: Difference + the number taken away must equal the starting number. If the check misses, the size of the miss shows which digit went wrong.

test.q: Kim works out 13.4 − 6.75, adds her answer to 6.75 as a check, and gets 14.4. What is the correct difference?
test.why: 13.40 − 6.75 = 6.65. Check: 6.65 + 6.75 = 13.40. (Kim's answer was 7.65, one too many, from not reducing the ones after borrowing.)

whyNot.0: 6.75 forgets to reduce the tenths digit after borrowing for the hundredths.
whyNot.1: 7.35 takes the smaller digit from the larger in each column instead of borrowing.
whyNot.3: 7.65 is Kim's answer; adding back gives 14.4, not 13.4.
